findings.text: Host dispatch makes two VM retirement services available. One opens retirement for a handle supplied by the host. The other closes retirement and reclaims resources for a handle already opened. Both are reachable through the central host call table.
Two shims bridge host calls to VM retirement services. Each takes a VM handle from the first argument register of the host context and places the service outcome back in the same register.

VM retirement has alive, retiring and gone states. Opening moves alive to retiring only for existing unreferenced entries not already retiring. Closing moves retiring to gone only for existing unreferenced entries already retiring. All other opening or closing attempts are rejected as invalid.

A VM table spin lock guards handle resolution and the retiring marker. Both retirement services hold it only for resolution plus marker check or update, leaving extended reclamation and donation outside the critical section.

Teardown handle resolution requires prior ownership of the table lock. It succeeds only for live handles with no outstanding references, otherwise it reports absence for missing handles and for handles still referenced.

Successful closing guarantees translation safety before identifier reuse, detachment of the table entry, return of table memory and per virtual CPU caches plus metadata toward host caches, release of host associations, and clearing of donated spans before handback apart from the table drain path which detaches without extra clearing.

Closing order affects safety. Translation safety must be established before the identifier can be reused, and detachment must happen while the table lock is held. After detachment the handle is invalid, so later opening or closing with the same handle must fail rather than revive the entry.

Retirement metadata spans hypervisor and host sides. The hypervisor side associates a pool, a retiring marker, a vector of virtual CPU pointers and a created count. The host side provides two teardown caches. Each hypervisor virtual CPU links a host counterpart and owns a personal cache.
Each allocation pool owns a spin lock covering free organization lookup, block removal, splitting and tracking marking for that pool.

Allocation promises a tracked block of the requested size class drawn from the smallest sufficient available class when one exists, with larger sources divided and remainders retained for later use. Exhaustion is signaled by absence.

Each pool organizes free memory as a family of lists keyed by size class up to a configured maximum. Linkage nodes live inside the page frames, permitting two way conversion between a list node and its page descriptor.

Page table reclamation ends with destroyed second stage mappings and an emptied source pool. Every recovered page has cleared tracking, resides in the caller supplied cache, and has been offered back to the host, with offer failures flagged.
Host dispatch publishes tracing controls for buffer load and unload, global activation, per CPU reader exchange, clock publication, per CPU reset, and event handling.

Tracing shims convert host registers to service inputs. Load takes address plus size, activation takes a boolean, reader exchange and reset take a CPU number, clock publication takes scaling plus epoch values, event activation takes identifier plus boolean, self test trigger takes an identifier. Status producing services report in the first argument register, while unload, clock publication and self test trigger report nothing.

Trace buffering shows empty versus populated, distinguished by zero versus nonzero backing size. Load is allowed only from empty and ends populated, with automatic return to empty on partial failure. Unload is allowed from either state and always ends empty.
One trace buffer spin lock serializes load, unload, activation, reader exchange and reset. Internal population and release helpers require the caller to already own it.

Tracing memory onboarding demands aligned nonempty windows, skips ownership transfer when protection is off, otherwise transfers from host for the usage duration. Backing is cleared on acquisition and on release, and the descriptor window is always released after a load attempt.

Host supplied tracing descriptors are untrusted when protection is on. Acceptance requires every per CPU entry to fit inside the donated window, total backing capacity to cover all claimed pages, and CPU numbers to be in range and to match table positions. With protection off the descriptor is accepted without checks.

Activation requires a populated buffer and applies uniformly to every CPU. Reader exchange and reset first validate the CPU number and then require a populated buffer before reaching the selected per CPU ring, keeping range failures distinct from absence of a loaded buffer.

Clock publication is accepted only after every per CPU ring is observed outside writing state, so all readers share the current bank at install time. The new scaling and epoch then become visible to later readers.
Trace backing is one contiguous window split in table order among per CPU rings. Each ring owns the slice matching its claimed page count, with the cursor advanced for the next ring.

Two shims expose virtual interrupt controller state handling. Each receives a host pointer in the first argument register, maps it to the hypervisor address space, and delegates to the matching save or restore service.
Saving preserves active priority state into the supplied CPU interface. Restoring leaves compatibility mode under a barrier before installing saved control and priority values.

A static table maps host call numbers to handler shims for initialization, virtual CPU control, translation maintenance, tracing, interrupt controller handling, and protected memory plus VM lifecycle. Entries derive from service names through a common macro over a shared handler function type.

Host call admission has pre and post initialization modes. Pre mode accepts only the early range. Post mode accepts only the later range, with finalization permitted in both yet self limiting after first use per CPU. Numbers outside the active window or hitting empty slots are reported as unsupported, otherwise success is marked before delegation.

Secure monitor interception rejects calls carrying trapped immediate bits or wide identifiers. Survivors are offered to power state handling, then firmware framework handling, then a forwarding path bracketed by exit and enter tracing. Control always resumes past the trapped instruction.

Power state relay chooses filtering and handling by configured version. Each version decides ownership with its own identifier test. Owned calls yield the handler outcome in the primary result register with the next three result registers cleared. Unowned identifiers are declined.

Legacy power handling forwards power down and migration with four registers through a secure monitor call returning the primary result. Power up and suspend follow dedicated paths. Remaining legacy numbers are reported as unsupported.

Call numbers arrive in register zero with hint bits ignored and a base removed before table lookup. Arguments arrive in low registers starting at one. Outcomes return in low registers starting at zero for dispatch and power relay layers and at one for shim layers. Secure monitor identifiers likewise arrive in register zero with hint bits ignored and high bits rejected.

Donated handback for teardown clears the aligned span before splitting it pagewise into the supplied cache with address translation, then detaches mappings without further clearing. Null detach requests are tolerated.
Host release covers the full created count, skipping empty slots and releasing both CPU association and vector state for each populated entry.
